pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** The Electromagnetic Spectrum

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS4 / GCSE Physics — 'Electromagnetic waves'):** the full EM spectrum radio→gamma; all EM waves are transverse, transfer energy, and travel at the same speed through a vacuum; practical uses across the seven regions and the hazardous (ionising) effects of UV, X-rays and gamma rays on tissue. NOTE: in England this is KS4 / GCSE content (typically 14–16; Oak National Academy places this exact lesson in Year 11), so the 12–13 placement here is an AMBITIOUS KS3→KS4 bridge — sequence it as an extension of the KS3 'colours and different frequencies of light'.

- **Standards — US (NGSS HS-PS4-4, with HS-PS4-1):** HS-PS4-4 — "evaluate the validity and reliability of claims in published materials of the effects that different frequencies of electromagnetic radiation have when absorbed by matter" (directly the uses/hazards/ionising strand); HS-PS4-1 supplies the wave relationships (v = fλ). These are US HIGH-SCHOOL expectations (14–18); NGSS has no middle-school full-spectrum PE, so again the 12–13 placement is early.

- **Operational details:** The EM spectrum is ONE family of the SAME phenomenon — transverse oscillations (ripples) in electric and magnetic fields — differing only in frequency/wavelength, NOT seven different 'things'. Seven regions in order of INCREASING frequency and energy (decreasing wavelength): RADIO → MICROWAVE → INFRARED → VISIBLE → ULTRAVIOLET → X-RAY → GAMMA (visible is a thin sliver; within it red = lowest frequency, violet = highest). ALL EM waves travel at the SAME speed in a vacuum, 3 × 10⁸ m/s — this common 'light speed' is what makes them one family. Higher frequency = higher energy = more able to damage cells/DNA; from UV upward the radiation is IONISING (UV, X-ray, gamma). Uses/hazards by band: radio (communication), microwave (cooking, phone/wifi), IR (thermal imaging, remotes), visible (sight, optical fibre), UV (sterilising, fluorescence; sunburn/skin cancer), X-ray (medical imaging; ionising), gamma (cancer treatment, sterilising; very hazardous). Harm is DOSE- and FREQUENCY-dependent — small exposures are harmless, radiation is natural (the Sun emits all seven ranges), and visible light IS radiation.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal). Requires abstract, relational reasoning across a 14-order-of-magnitude continuum plus the energy–ionisation causal chain — demanding at 12–13. Success = order the seven regions by frequency, state that all EM waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, give at least one use AND one hazard per region, and explain WHY higher-frequency waves are more dangerous (more energy → ionising → cell/DNA damage). Watch for the four sticky errors: regions as different phenomena, 'all radiation dangerous/unnatural', 'light isn't radiation', and 'radio waves are sound'.
bestPractices: Reframe the LANGUAGE from 'kinds' to 'frequency ranges' (Oak National Academy): every region is the SAME phenomenon — EM waves in electric and magnetic fields — at a different frequency. This is the single most important corrective; say it repeatedly and model the vocabulary.

Refute the danger/naturalness myths explicitly: counter 'all radiation is dangerous' and 'all radiation is man-made' — the Sun emits all seven ranges and visible light IS radiation; teach harm as DOSE- and FREQUENCY-dependent, with an ionising threshold around UV.

Make IONISATION the organising principle for hazards: higher frequency → higher energy → from UV upward it can ionise atoms and damage DNA — so 'why are some more dangerous?' becomes a causal chain, not a memorised danger list.

Use beyond-the-visible demonstrations (Oak, verified): a ray box + prism shows visible light IS a range of frequencies; detect invisible IR with a thermometer placed just beyond the red end or a hand near a hot non-glowing object; a blacklight shows UV fluorescence — proving the invisible bands are real radiation on one continuum.

Run an ordering activity — a card-sort or 'clothesline' of the seven bands by frequency, then match uses and hazards to each — and let pupils invent their OWN mnemonic for the order (self-generated aids improve retention).

Teach the SCALE honestly: wavelengths span roughly 14 orders of magnitude from radio to gamma, so no single linear drawing can show it to scale — name the limitation rather than implying the bands are similar sizes.
Directly separate wave-TYPE confusions: EM waves are transverse and need NO medium (they cross a vacuum), which counters both 'radio waves are sound' and 'all waves need a medium'.
Consolidate with a per-band chart (frequency/wavelength · use · hazard) built collaboratively across the lesson.
keyRepresentations: The linear EM spectrum strip: seven bands radio→gamma with arrows for increasing frequency/energy and decreasing wavelength, and visible shown as a thin colour sliver.

A 'same phenomenon, different frequency' diagram: the identical electric/magnetic field ripple drawn at different wavelengths and labelled with band names — built to dissolve the 'different kinds' idea.
Per-band chart: region · frequency/wavelength · use · hazard.
The ionising-threshold marker (~UV) dividing non-ionising (radio→visible) from ionising (UV, X-ray, gamma).
Beyond-the-visible demonstrations: prism spectrum + thermometer-just-past-red (IR) + blacklight fluorescence (UV).
A card-sort / clothesline ordering line plus a student-generated mnemonic for the sequence.
commonMisconceptions: The regions are different phenomena / different 'kinds' of thing, unrelated to each other and to visible light — rather than one family differing only in frequency (the #1 misconception, per Oak).
'Light is not radiation' — failing to recognise visible light as part of the EM spectrum.
'All radiation is dangerous' and 'all radiation is man-made/unnatural' — whereas the Sun emits all seven ranges and low-frequency EM is largely harmless; harm is dose- and frequency-dependent.
Conflating ionising with non-ionising radiation (thinking radio/microwave damage DNA the way gamma does), and confusing irradiation with contamination.
'Radio waves are sound' — misidentifying an EM wave as a mechanical/sound wave.
'All waves need a medium' — not realising EM waves travel through a vacuum.
Believing EM waves travel at different speeds (e.g. higher-frequency = slower) — all travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum.
'If something makes EM radiation, it glows' — expecting all EM emission to be visible, when visible is only a thin sliver.

learn.summary: Learners build the electromagnetic spectrum as ONE phenomenon — transverse ripples in electric and magnetic fields — that differs only by frequency/wavelength, not as seven separate 'kinds' of thing. The core correction is linguistic and conceptual: say 'frequency ranges', not 'kinds'. Learners order the seven regions by increasing frequency (radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-ray → gamma), learn that all EM waves travel at 3×10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, give a use and a hazard per band, and reason WHY higher-frequency waves are more dangerous via the causal chain higher frequency → higher energy → ionising (from ~UV upward) → cell/DNA damage. Harm is dose- AND frequency-dependent; radiation is natural (the Sun emits all seven ranges) and visible light IS radiation. This is normally KS4/GCSE / US high-school content, so at age 12–13 it is an ambitious extension of the KS3 'colours and frequencies of light' work.

activities.title: Sweep the spectrum: one wave, many frequencies
feedback: If a learner expects the wave to change into a different 'type' as they drag: highlight that it is the identical field ripple throughout — only its frequency and wavelength change (together, since their product stays equal to c) — so there is one family, not seven separate things.

If a learner says the faster-dragged or higher-frequency wave moves faster: point to the pinned 3×10⁸ m/s readout — speed in a vacuum is constant; what changes is frequency and wavelength (their product stays equal to c).

If a learner treats radio as capable of ionising/DNA damage: radio and microwave photons lack the per-photon energy to ionise atoms, so they cause no ionising (DNA-damaging) harm at any dose — ionising harm only begins around UV. (Very intense non-ionising radiation can still heat tissue, but that is a separate thermal effect, not ionisation.)
If a learner thinks only the bands they can see are 'real': note that visible is a thin sliver and the invisible bands are equally real radiation on the same continuum.
activities.rationale: Making the single most important correction ('frequency ranges, not kinds') experiential through a continuous morph ties frequency, energy, speed and hazard together in one gesture rather than as a memorised list; an interactive slider lets learners test the 'faster/slower' and 'all dangerous' misconceptions directly.
sourceClaims: Target misconception: the different 'kinds' of EM radiation are treated as different phenomena to each other and to visible light; pupils also think all radiation is dangerous, none is natural, and that light is not radiation. Correction: each is the SAME phenomenon (ripples in electric/magnetic fields) at different frequencies — refer to frequency ranges, not 'kinds'. The Sun emits all seven ranges. Order radio→microwave→IR→visible→UV→X-ray→gamma; beyond-visible demos (prism, thermometer IR, blacklight UV). This is a KS4 (Year 11) lesson.

Recurring EMR misconceptions: conflating ionizing and non-ionizing radiation, believing all radiation is harmful, and confusing irradiation with contamination; these persist among public, students and educators and are fed by inadequate education and media misrepresentation.
learnerActions: Drag a frequency control from the radio end up to the gamma end and watch a single electric/magnetic field wave visibly shorten as frequency rises, while the band name, wavelength and an example source update as you move.
Pause at each of the seven bands and say aloud: 'This is the same wave as the others, just at a higher/lower frequency.'
Watch a speed readout that stays pinned at 3×10⁸ m/s across the whole sweep, and explain in your own words why 'higher frequency = faster' must be wrong.

Move into the ultraviolet range and observe an 'IONISING' indicator switch on (the real threshold lies inside the UV band rather than exactly at the visible/UV edge, so treat the switch point as approximate); describe what newly becomes possible (ionising atoms, damaging DNA) past that point.

Adjust a dose/exposure control at a low-frequency band (radio) and at a high-frequency band (gamma) and compare the ionising harm: it rises with exposure AND frequency at gamma, while radio stays at zero ionising harm regardless of dose.
activities.intendedInsight: The seven 'kinds' of radiation are one continuous phenomenon differing only in frequency and wavelength; all EM waves share one vacuum speed; ionising danger rises with frequency/energy (ionising from ~UV up) and the amount of ionising damage also depends on dose — so low-frequency radiation like radio does not ionise atoms or damage DNA even at high dose.

activities.title: Order the bands and match uses and hazards
feedback: If the order is reversed or a band is misplaced: anchor to the familiar visible band (red = lowest frequency, violet = highest) and build outward — infrared just below red, ultraviolet just above violet.
If a learner labels radio or microwave as ionising: reinforce that ionising begins around UV; radio and microwave carry too little energy per photon to ionise.
If a learner can list uses but not hazards (or vice versa): prompt for the missing half so every band carries both a use and a hazard.
Praise a self-generated mnemonic specifically and have the learner test it by rebuilding the order without the cards.
activities.rationale: An ordering task plus use/hazard matching consolidates recall of the sequence and the band-specific facts; placing the ionising threshold makes hazard an organising principle rather than a memorised danger list, and inventing one's own mnemonic (rather than receiving a supplied one) may support retention.
sourceClaims: 'If something makes EM radiation it glows' is false (visible is only a thin sliver); 'all waves need a medium' is false (only mechanical waves do); ionising begins around UV; card-sort/clothesline ordering activity and the ~14-orders-of-magnitude scale caveat.

US national anchor: evaluate claims about the effects that different frequencies of EM radiation have when absorbed by matter (uses/hazards, ionisation); wave relationships v = fλ. These are high-school expectations.
learnerActions: Drag the seven bands into order of increasing frequency (radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-ray → gamma), e.g. as a card-sort or a 'clothesline' line.

For each band, match at least one real use and one hazard: radio (communication; very intense exposure can heat body tissue, but it is not ionising), microwave (cooking, phone/wifi; internal heating of body tissue at high intensity), infrared (thermal imaging, remote controls; skin burns), visible (sight, optical fibre; eye damage from very bright light or lasers), ultraviolet (sterilising, fluorescence; sunburn, eye damage, skin cancer), X-ray (medical imaging; ionising, can damage cells/DNA), gamma (cancer treatment, sterilising; ionising, very hazardous).
Mark where the ionising threshold falls (~UV) and label which bands are ionising (UV, X-ray, gamma) versus non-ionising (radio → visible).
Invent your OWN mnemonic for the seven-band order and use it to rebuild the sequence from memory.
activities.intendedInsight: The spectrum is a fixed ordered sequence of frequency ranges, each with characteristic uses and hazards, and the ionising threshold around UV separates the tissue-ionising end from the non-ionising low-frequency end.

activities.title: Beyond the visible: showing the invisible bands are real
feedback: If a learner assumes nothing is there beyond red/violet because they see nothing: point to any thermometer rise beyond red compared with the control, or to the fluorescence — an invisible band is producing a detectable effect.
If a learner still treats visible light as separate from 'radiation': note that the prism shows visible light is itself a frequency range, continuous with infrared below and ultraviolet above.
activities.rationale: Physical detection of infrared and ultraviolet gives direct evidence that the invisible bands are real radiation, countering the 'it must glow' and 'light isn't radiation' misconceptions through observation rather than assertion.
sourceClaims: Target misconception: the different 'kinds' of EM radiation are treated as different phenomena to each other and to visible light; pupils also think all radiation is dangerous, none is natural, and that light is not radiation. Correction: each is the SAME phenomenon (ripples in electric/magnetic fields) at different frequencies — refer to frequency ranges, not 'kinds'. The Sun emits all seven ranges. Order radio→microwave→IR→visible→UV→X-ray→gamma; beyond-visible demos (prism, thermometer IR, blacklight UV). This is a KS4 (Year 11) lesson.

'If something makes EM radiation it glows' is false (visible is only a thin sliver); 'all waves need a medium' is false (only mechanical waves do); ionising begins around UV; card-sort/clothesline ordering activity and the ~14-orders-of-magnitude scale caveat.
learnerActions: Use a ray box and prism (or observe this demonstrated) to spread white light into a spectrum, confirming that visible light IS itself a range of frequencies.

Place a thermometer (ideally with a blackened bulb, and a bright source such as sunlight) just beyond the red end of the spectrum and compare it with a control thermometer outside the beam. Any rise may be small and is not guaranteed with a weak ray box. Alternatively, hold a hand beside (not above) a hot but non-glowing object to feel infrared you cannot see.
Shine an ultraviolet 'blacklight' on a fluorescing material to reveal UV by its effect.
Write a short conclusion: 'The invisible bands are real radiation on the same continuum as visible light — we just cannot see them.'
activities.intendedInsight: Invisible EM bands are genuinely present radiation, detectable by their effects; visible light is only a thin sliver of a much wider continuum, so 'if it makes EM radiation it glows' is false.

activities.title: Same speed, different energy: the star-burst reasoning task
feedback: If a learner picks gamma 'because it carries the most energy': separate the ideas — energy/frequency vary across the spectrum, but vacuum speed does not; light from all stars arrives on time regardless of colour.

If a learner picks radio 'because its wavelength is longer': apply v = fλ with v = c — a long wavelength simply pairs with a low frequency; the product (speed) is identical, so longer does not mean faster.

If a learner says the vacuum stops or slows the waves, or that they need a medium: contrast with sound — EM waves are self-propagating electric/magnetic oscillations that cross empty space, which is exactly why we see the Sun and stars while space is silent.

Full-credit response: says 'together', explains that all EM waves share one vacuum speed independent of frequency/energy, infers that radio must have the much longer wavelength, and keeps 'same speed' distinct from 'different energy/hazard'.
activities.rationale: A two-tier diagnostic that forces the reason discriminates the correct single-speed model from the seductive 'more energetic → faster' and 'longer wavelength → faster' models, and from the 'EM needs a medium' confusion; requiring justification prevents 'together' being a lucky guess.
sourceClaims: Students frequently misidentify radio waves as sound waves rather than as part of the electromagnetic spectrum (pilot survey of 225 high-school physics students).

US national anchor: evaluate claims about the effects that different frequencies of EM radiation have when absorbed by matter (uses/hazards, ionisation); wave relationships v = fλ. These are high-school expectations.
learnerActions: Consider: a distant exploding star emits a burst of radio waves AND a burst of gamma rays at the very same instant, both crossing empty space to Earth. Decide which arrives first — radio, gamma, or together — and write WHY.
State the defining rule in your own words: all EM waves travel at 3×10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, regardless of frequency or energy.
Given equal speed but very different frequencies for radio and gamma, work out what MUST differ about their wavelengths (use v = fλ with v fixed at c).
Explain, using the energy/ionisation chain, why gamma is far more dangerous to living tissue than radio even though both travel at the same speed.
Explain why the Sun is silent in space yet blazes with light — what that shows about EM waves versus sound.
activities.intendedInsight: Speed in a vacuum is the same for all EM waves and is independent of frequency, energy and wavelength; what varies along the spectrum is frequency/energy (hence hazard) and wavelength — and EM waves, unlike sound, need no medium.

activities.title: Myth-busting radiation with an expert in role
feedback: If a learner holds 'all radiation is dangerous': the Sun emits across the whole spectrum (though the atmosphere blocks its X-rays, gamma rays and much of its UV), and we live in its visible light and infrared every day; harm is dose- and frequency-dependent, with ionising (tissue-damaging) effects beginning around UV.
If a learner says 'radio waves are sound': radio is an EM (transverse, no medium needed) wave travelling at c in a vacuum; sound is a mechanical wave needing a medium — they are different phenomena.
If a learner conflates ionising with non-ionising: only UV and above can ionise atoms and damage DNA; radio and microwave cannot do this however intense.
activities.rationale: This topic is unusually myth-laden with documented media-driven misconceptions, so dialogue that answers learners' own safety questions can motivate and address the danger/naturalness myths; it is a supplement and does not by itself build the ordered-spectrum structure or verify recall.
sourceClaims: Recurring EMR misconceptions: conflating ionizing and non-ionizing radiation, believing all radiation is harmful, and confusing irradiation with contamination; these persist among public, students and educators and are fed by inadequate education and media misrepresentation.
Students frequently misidentify radio waves as sound waves rather than as part of the electromagnetic spectrum (pilot survey of 225 high-school physics students).
learnerActions: Ask an in-role expert (e.g. a radiographer, radio engineer or astronomer) your real radiation-safety questions: 'Is my phone dangerous?', 'Is sunlight radiation?', 'Why can't I see infrared?'
For each answer, restate the key idea back: same phenomenon at different frequencies, and harm that depends on dose AND frequency.
Sort a set of statements into true/false to surface and challenge the myths, e.g. 'all radiation is man-made', 'all radiation is dangerous', 'light is not radiation', 'radio waves are sound'.
activities.intendedInsight: Everyday radiation fears often stem from media misrepresentation; most low-frequency EM exposure is harmless, much radiation is natural (e.g. sunlight), visible light is radiation, and radio waves are EM (not sound).

constraints: This is normally KS4/GCSE (England, typically 14–16; Oak National Academy places this exact lesson in Year 11) and US high-school content (NGSS HS-PS4-4/HS-PS4-1, ages 14–18); at age 12–13 treat it as an ambitious extension of KS3 'colours and different frequencies of light', not core-level content.

Teach harm as dose- AND frequency-dependent, with an ionising threshold around UV — do not imply all radiation is dangerous or all is man-made. Keep 'same vacuum speed' distinct from 'different energy/hazard'. Scope 'radio is safe' claims to ionisation (no DNA damage at any dose); do not state that non-ionising radiation has literally no effect.

The spectrum spans well over a dozen orders of magnitude in wavelength from radio to gamma (the exact figure depends on where the band edges are drawn), so no single linear drawing can show the bands to scale — name this limitation rather than implying the bands are similar in size.

A labelled spectrum strip with tap-to-reveal uses/hazards is an effective reference and an ordering/matching quiz is an effective recall/diagnostic check, but recognition and reveal formats do not by themselves elicit the learner's own construction of the 'one continuous phenomenon' insight; pair them with the sweep/ordering and reasoning tasks.
The expert-dialogue activity is a motivational supplement; it does not build the ordered-spectrum structure or verify recall on its own.
Use consistent language: 'frequency ranges' rather than 'kinds'. Within visible, red = lowest frequency, violet = highest.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving any activity was tested.

Of the six cited sources, only the Oak National Academy source is marked verified:true; the EJSEE misconceptions review, SERP SciGen E5.3, the Tabor-Morris ERIC pilot, NGSS, and the DfE subject content are marked verified:false. Confidence in specific misconception frequencies and the ~14-orders-of-magnitude figure rests on unverified sources.

The pedagogy claim that learner-generated mnemonics 'improve retention' (and 'better than supplied ones') is not supported by any cited sources[].claim; it has been rendered as 'may support retention' pending evidence.

Self-audit of physics: 3×10⁸ m/s vacuum speed, the radio→microwave→IR→visible→UV→X-ray→gamma ordering by increasing frequency/decreasing wavelength, v = fλ reasoning (fixed c implies longer wavelength pairs with lower frequency), the ~UV ionising threshold, and the 'same speed, different energy' star-burst answer were checked for internal consistency and are coherent as stated.

The original designNotes phrase 'radio at any dose stays safe' was an over-broad simplification; it has been rescoped throughout to 'no ionising/DNA damage at any dose', because very intense non-ionising radiation can still cause thermal heating — a separate effect outside this topic's scope. This scoping is now consistent across activity[0], activity[4] and the constraints.

The 'danger meter'/dose control and the field-wave morph are concrete interaction examples offered to make the mechanism tangible; they are optional illustrations, not mandatory mechanisms, and should not be read as the only way to teach the continuum.

The claim that the slider-morph is the only way the 'one family' idea becomes 'felt' has been softened: a fixed labelled diagram can still teach the ordering and facts; the interactive sweep is proposed for its specific affordance (continuous linking of frequency, speed and hazard), not as universally necessary.

probeDeeper: Sunlight (visible) and the Sun's X-rays leave the Sun together. Do they reach us at the same moment? Use your rule to decide.
If radio and gamma travel at the same speed but have very different frequencies, what MUST be different about their wavelengths?
The Sun is silent in space but blazing with light. What does that tell you about how EM waves travel compared with sound?
Gamma rays are far more dangerous to living tissue than radio waves. If they travel at the same speed, what IS different about them that makes gamma so harmful?
assess.correctAnswer: They arrive TOGETHER. All electromagnetic waves — radio, light, gamma, everything between — travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s). Frequency and energy differ across the spectrum, but speed in empty space does not, so both bursts cover the same distance in the same time.

errorPatterns.pattern: Higher frequency/energy means faster — 'gamma rays are the most powerful, so they get here first'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: State and use the defining fact: every EM wave travels at c in a vacuum. Separate the ideas — energy/frequency vary along the spectrum, speed (in vacuum) does not. Anchor with light from all stars arriving on time regardless of colour.
errorPatterns.distractor: The gamma rays arrive first because they carry the most energy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses gamma; equates the wave's energy or 'strength' with how fast it moves.

errorPatterns.pattern: Longer wavelength travels faster — 'radio waves are huge and spread out, so they race ahead'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use v = fλ with fixed v = c: a long wavelength simply pairs with a low frequency; the PRODUCT (speed) is identical. Longer does not mean faster.
errorPatterns.distractor: The radio waves arrive first because their wavelength is much longer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses radio; reasons from wavelength size to speed.

errorPatterns.pattern: EM waves need a medium like sound does — 'nothing can travel across truly empty space, so neither really gets here / they slow down in the vacuum'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast sharply with sound: EM waves are self-propagating electric/magnetic oscillations that need NO medium — which is exactly why we see the Sun and stars across empty space, while space is silent.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In probing, claims the waves need something to travel through, or that a vacuum stops or slows them; conflates EM waves with sound.

responseLevels.gap: Chooses gamma (energy = fast) or radio (long = fast); ties speed to frequency, energy or wavelength.
responseLevels.full: Says together AND explains all EM waves share one vacuum speed independent of frequency/energy; transfers cleanly — sunlight and X-rays arrive together, infers the wavelength contrast from equal speed, and separates 'same speed' from 'different energy/hazard'.
responseLevels.partial: Says 'together' but justifies weakly — recites 'they all go at the speed of light' without separating speed from frequency/energy, and falters on transfer (e.g. still hints the vacuum slows them, or can't say what must differ about wavelength).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A distant exploding star sends out a burst of radio waves AND a burst of gamma rays at the very same instant. Both travel across empty space to Earth. Which burst arrives first — the radio waves, the gamma rays, or do they arrive together — and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The seductive wrong model is 'more energetic → faster', which predicts gamma first; a rival wrong model is 'longer wavelength → faster', predicting radio first. Only the child who holds 'all EM waves share one vacuum speed' says together. Tier 2 forces the reason, so 'together' can't be a lucky guess — the child must separate speed from frequency/energy.
